One Tile, Four Answers

A segmentation raster goes in. RT indexes it, fetches the current OpenStreetMap data for that exact footprint, and runs the four solutions that need no model. Every picture below is output from that run — not a mockup.

The run

What went in

rasteraza AOI — 8,509 × 8,405 px at 0.122 m/px, 1.07 km², 100% classified
regions95,170 connected components — the only spatial unit RT had
OSM ways4,648 — 4,361 buildings, 255 roads, 14 footways, 19 named streets
blocks98 road-bounded, 54 of them bounded by at least one named street
co-registrationREGISTERED — 63.9% of ST's road pixels fall inside the OSM corridor at zero shift; the best-fit shift is 2.08 m

The close-ups below are a 1,800 px window — 220 m of ground — chosen automatically as the densest mix of mapped street and labelled building in the AOI.

Plate 01

What the segmenter saw

47 classes, colourised. No imagery is involved anywhere in this pipeline — this raster is the whole input.

Plate 02

The second map, laid over it

OSM ways buffered by a width taken from each way's own tags, burned onto the raster's grid. This picture is the co-registration check that a number cannot make: a shift test catches a uniform offset, and only the eye catches a rotation or a mis-placed tile.

Plate 03

The ground, partitioned

Blocks are the complement of the corridor: the ground the street network encloses. Not cadastral parcels, and no claim that a block is homogeneous — what is inside one is exactly the question the labels answer.

Plate 04 · S4

The difference the join makes

Wheeled-vehicle trafficability over the same window, without and with the OSM overlay. Drag the handle.

with OSM segmentation only
  • passable
  • slow going
  • impassable

On the right, the segmentation alone: the streets are labelled Shadow and MaralBadlands, whose trafficability is the 0.5 default, so the densest street network in the AOI reads as mediocre going and the yellow route fragments. On the left, the same computation with the corridor as a known-passable overlay and mapped footprints as blockers. The overlay moved 29.9% of this window.

Slope still applies. A mapped road up a 40° face is a mapped road a tank cannot climb; the overlay says the surface is there, not that the vehicle can get up it.

Plate 05 · S4

One more product, same overlay

A fire fuel plate stood beside this one, showing OSM subtracting mapped footprints from a fuel-load map. That product has since been retired, together with drainage. The shipped set is now trafficability, concealment, built fabric and change volatility — the two replacements have no plate here because this run predates them.

Plate 06 · S1

A finding, close up

The reference checks are the only ones that can contradict a label using something outside the label raster. Here is one of 75 on this AOI.

[reference-gap] OSM maps unnamed residential (way 41255009, residential)
here; ST labels 12% of the corridor as a road. Under it:
MaralBadlands 33%, Shadow 17%, DirtRoad 12%

The tag is the resolution, not a verdict. OSM is the authority on whether a street exists, so the corridor is taken as real; ST is the authority on what the surface looks like now. So this reads as a surface that changed or a label that was missed — and never as “the segmenter is wrong”, which is a claim neither map is in a position to make.

Run it

Your own tile

$ segmap playground
RT playground on http://127.0.0.1:8011/
  upload a segmentation raster; OSM is fetched live for its footprint

A GeoTIFF carries its own georeference and needs nothing else. A .png or .npy is asked for the bounding box it covers, rather than being joined to a guess — a join to the wrong ground produces a beautiful partition of somewhere else. A real Smart Terrain export whose ids are sparse wire ids wants its class-mapping JSON alongside.

Each run states its megapixel budget, the UTC time OSM was fetched, and the co-registration verdict before it shows a single number. Every panel is the CLI's own renderer, so anything on the page comes back from segmap solve … --osm.
